title: Europe is redrawing its textile investment map, Bangladesh must shift its bet
summary: Europe’s textile industry is quietly changing where capital goes. Investment is moving beyond physical expansion toward circular infrastructure, digital supply chains, low-carbon processing, and advan...
content: Europe’s textile industry is quietly changing where capital goes. Investment is moving beyond physical expansion toward circular infrastructure, digital supply chains, low-carbon processing, and advanced material research. Bangladesh, meanwhile, continues to invest heavily in basic capacity. This widening gap could weaken its Ready-Made Garment (RMG) export position in Europe unless manufacturers shift from volume-led growth to value-led investment. Figure: European Commission estimates that reaching just 10% recycling could save 440,000 metric tons of annual carbon emissions and 8.8 billion cubic meters of water. The clearest signal is Europe’s growing focus on textile waste as a strategic raw material. A Boston Consulting Group and ReHubs study estimates that scaling textile-to-textile recycling to 15% by 2035 will require €8 billion–€11 billion in capital expenditure, plus €5 billion–€6.5 billion in annual operating costs. The European Commission estimates that reaching just 10% recycling could save 440,000 metric tons of annual carbon emissions and 8.8 billion cubic meters of water. Digitalization and clean manufacturing are also attracting capital. EU-backed programs are supporting Industry 4.0 automation, digital tracking and circular design, while Horizon Europe has allocated €450 million for biodegradable polymers and closed-loop synthetic recycling. The Digital Product Passport (DPP) is reinforcing this direction by making product-level data, fiber origin and traceability increasingly central to market access. Recent trade data shows the gap. Bangladesh’s apparel exports to the EU fell 16.43% to €8.64 billion in H1 2026. Volume fell 8.22% and unit prices dropped 8.94% to €13.88 per kilogram. title: Bangladesh’s garments industry at a turning point (Part: 1)
summary: For much of the past several months, the conversation around Bangladesh’s garments industry has been dominated by crisis. Gas shortages are disrupting production, electricity remains uncertain in ma...
content: For much of the past several months, the conversation around Bangladesh’s garments industry has been dominated by crisis. Gas shortages are disrupting production, electricity remains uncertain in many industrial areas, geopolitical tensions are affecting energy and shipping routes, costs are rising and international buyers are becoming increasingly cautious about delivery reliability. These concerns are real, and anyone working closely with the industry knows that they are not simply issues being discussed in boardrooms. They are being felt on factory floors, in production planning meetings and in the financial decisions manufacturers have to make every day. Yet there is another side of the Bangladesh story that deserves equal attention. Beneath the immediate difficulties is an industry that has spent more than three decades building something that is extremely difficult to reproduce elsewhere: a large-scale manufacturing ecosystem supported by experienced workers, established supplier networks, increasingly sophisticated factories and a growing culture of social and environmental responsibility. The question now is not simply whether the industry can survive another difficult period. The more important question is whether Bangladesh can use this period of pressure to build a stronger and more competitive industrial model. Bangladesh’s position in the global apparel market has never really been based on cheap labor alone. Price is important, of course, but an international buyer placing a large order needs much more than a competitive FOB. The buyer needs confidence that a factory can maintain quality across large volumes, manage raw materials, meet technical requirements, comply with social and environmental standards and deliver on time. title: Madagascar apparel sector shifts from cost to resilience
summary: Madagascar is seeking to strengthen its apparel industry by combining its low-cost manufacturing advantage with stronger compliance, value addition, and supply chain resilience. Figure:Madagascar ran...
content: Madagascar is seeking to strengthen its apparel industry by combining its low-cost manufacturing advantage with stronger compliance, value addition, and supply chain resilience. Figure:Madagascar ranked second among sub-Saharan African textile and apparel exporters to the US and first to the EU in 2023. The textile and apparel sector remains a major part of the economy, supporting about 180,000 formal jobs and accounting for roughly 25% of the country’s exports, according to the International Labour Organization. The United States remains an important market. Madagascar ranked second among sub-Saharan African textile and apparel exporters to the US and first to the EU in 2023, according to the US International Trade Administration. The sector also provided more than 400,000 direct and indirect jobs in 2025, reflecting its wider economic impact. But the industry faces a major trade challenge. The end of African Growth and Opportunity Act preferences and changes in US tariffs have increased pressure on export competitiveness. In January 2026, Madagascar’s textile employers warned that about 7,000 direct jobs could be at risk from reduced orders. The response is increasingly focused on diversification and higher value production. content: KnitMesh Technologies has showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe in London, highlighting the role of physical protection in layered defence against hostile and unauthorised drones. Executive Chairman Lew Bingham and Security and Defence Business Development Manager Andrew De-Gol represented the UK manufacturer during the two-day event, meeting defence and security professionals, existing customers and potential international partners. Developed, manufactured and tested by KnitMesh Technologies in the UK, DroneStop is a high-performance Counter-UAS solution designed to help mitigate risks associated with hostile and unauthorised drones. The system uses lightweight, high-strength stainless steel knitted mesh to provide a passive physical barrier that can operate alongside electronic and procedural countermeasures. It requires no power, jamming or radio frequency interference and can be incorporated into existing security infrastructure for temporary or permanent installations. Executive Chairman Lew Bingham (right) and Security and Defence Business Development Manager Andrew De-Gol at Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe in London. © KnitMesh Technologies Potential applications include military and defence facilities, critical national infrastructure, prisons and other secure environments where physical protection against drones is required. KnitMesh said discussions at the London event demonstrated growing interest in physical barriers as an additional layer within wider Counter-UAS strategies. “It was a very worthwhile few days at the European Counter-UAS Conference in London, with plenty of good conversations, shared experiences and lessons learned from across the defence and security community,” said De-Gol. Karotoa plans to generate 6 MW of solar power through rooftop installations across the factory. Solar panels have already been installed in one unit. For the textile sector of Bangladesh, this approach has growing importance as factories face pressure to reduce dependence on fossil fuels, manage energy costs, and respond to decarbonization expectations from global buyers. According to industry reports, Bangladesh already has one of the strongest green-factory bases in the world, with 290 LEED-certified RMG factories recorded by July 2026. Karotoa is also building water management into its core production model. 6 acres of land have been developed on the premises. Water from the pond will be treated and reused in the factory, while rainwater will be captured, purified, and returned to the water system. The event’s theme, “The world is moving forward – where is Europe?”, outlined the industry’s current landscape: increasing competition from Asia, coupled with challenging business conditions in Europe, has led to significant declines in order intake and turnover in recent years. Although the turnover forecast for 2026 had to be revised downwards to -14 per cent (nominal), order intake appears to be stabilising. “The discussions and workshops at our General Assembly clearly demonstrated that our industry is in the midst of profound change. The challenges are considerable, yet we possess the innovative strength, the expertise and the technological leadership to actively shape these changes. Together, we will work to support our customers even more effectively throughout the entire lifecycle of their machinery and equipment, to capitalise on the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence, and to strengthen the competitiveness of the European textile machinery industry in the long term. Not analysing it, not mining it, not drilling down to first principles,” he says. content: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) President Mahmud Hasan Khan today urged Pakistan to increase imports of Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceutical products to reduce the bilateral trade imbalance and expand economic cooperation between the two countries. He made the call during a meeting with Pakistan High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider at the BGMEA office in the city, said a press release. At the meeting, the BGMEA president also emphasised increasing imports of chemicals and dyes from Pakistan for Bangladesh’s garment industry, highlighting the potential for expanding trade in both directions. Although Bangladesh imports a significant volume of goods from Pakistan, including raw materials for the garment industry, its exports to the neighbouring country remain comparatively low, the release said. The BGMEA president called for greater efforts to address the imbalance by exploring new export opportunities and strengthening commercial ties. Pakistan high commissioner expressed keen interest in the proposals and assured that necessary steps would be taken to promote bilateral trade. The meeting also discussed arranging visits by high-level business delegations from both countries to identify new opportunities and establish direct commercial links. Haider said the Pakistan High Commission would facilitate business-to-business meetings and matchmaking sessions with leading Pakistani importers, brands, buyers and business associations if a Bangladeshi delegation comprising garment and other sector exporters visited Pakistan. content: BGMEA hosted an introductory session on 30 September for representatives from member factories to learn more about the BGMEA × AWARE Digital Product Passport (DPP) Pilot and understand how their factories can participate. The pilot aims to help participating factories prepare for the growing demand for transparent, verifiable production and traceability data, particularly as the EU moves toward Digital Product Passport requirements for textiles. Through the pilot, participating factories can explore a verified, producer-owned record of production data, supported by AWARE’s Crypto TC technology. The model is designed to provide a single source of verified information that can be shared across buyer relationships, while keeping production data under the factory’s ownership. The pilot also offers guided onboarding and training, data collection and DPP creation, review and validation, with the DPP creation cost fully covered during the pilot period. The session provided factory representatives with an opportunity to better understand the pilot, its potential benefits, participation process and how digital traceability can support the Bangladesh RMG sector’s transition toward greater transparency and EU market readiness. BGMEA looks forward to supporting member factories in exploring practical digital solutions that can strengthen traceability, transparency and competitiveness in the evolving global apparel landscape. content: The rapid adoption of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is beginning to have a measurable impact on the fashion industry, changing clothing sizes, purchasing patterns and even the balance between online and physical retail. Drugs including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro are already being associated with what has been dubbed the ‘Ozempic economy’, as significant changes in body weight force consumers to replace clothing and reconsider what and how they buy. Research from PwC suggests the impact on apparel could be substantial. Some 73% of US GLP-1 users surveyed reported a meaningful change in clothing size, while apparel spending was 9.9% higher after users had been taking the drugs for six-to-eight months. The effects are also becoming apparent in the UK. PwC estimates that around three million British adults currently use GLP-1 medications, with 40% of users surveyed saying they were spending more on clothing. One consequence could be an unexpected revival in physical clothes shopping. A US survey of 500 GLP-1 users by returns management specialist ReturnPro found that 69% had become less confident about online sizing as their bodies changed, making the ability to try garments on in stores more important. Some 71% said they were buying more apparel as their size changed, while 58% reported increased spending on premium or higher-priced clothing. More than half expected their clothing expenditure to rise further once their weight had stabilised. The trend presents challenges as well as opportunities for retailers. ReturnPro found that 65% of GLP-1 consumers surveyed were buying several sizes of the same garment with the intention of returning those that did not fit, while 43% said their frequency of apparel returns had increased. content: Young Labels Ltd and Japan-based Toska-Bano’k Co Ltd have started local production of the FasBano’k garment tagging system in Bangladesh, expanding the availability of the Japanese-developed technology for the country’s apparel and textile industry. The system and its local production were presented at an opening ceremony held yesterday (25 September) at the Bangla-Bano’k factory in Dhaka, bringing together representatives from Japanese organisations, Toska-Bano’k and Young Labels, according to a press release. Embassy of Japan in Bangladesh First Secretary Saori Fujimoto; Daisuke Arai of Jetro Dhaka; Yasuyuki Marahashi of Jica; Toska-Bano’k Co Ltd President Masao Terunuma; and Young Labels Ltd Managing Director S Mahmud (Mujbik) attended the event. FasBano’k is designed to attach tags using a dedicated hand tool together with specially designed tag loops or string fasteners. The system provides an alternative to conventional processes in which workers manually string or tie individual tags during garment finishing. Toska-Bano’k says its fastening mechanism allows tags to be attached more quickly than conventional manual methods, with the system designed for continuous operation. The technology can be used for garments, footwear and other textile products. Material options The tagging system is available with a range of material options, including recycled plastic, polyester, cotton, jute and paper. The different material choices allow manufacturers and brands to select tagging materials according to product specifications, sourcing requirements and sustainability considerations. For applications using recycled materials, Transaction Certificates (TCs) can also be provided where applicable for buyers and manufacturers requiring documentation relating to recycled content

content: By K. Gopalakrishnan With resilient FY26 performance, new capacity coming on stream in India and Africa, deeper vertical integration and a sharper focus on higher-value apparel, Gokaldas Exports is positioning itself for the next phase of growth in the global apparel supply chain. SivaramaKrishnan Ganapathi, Vice chairman & Managing Director, Gokaldas Exports For Gokaldas Exports Ltd., FY26 was a year of navigating considerable external turbulence while continuing to build the capabilities required for longer-term growth. Geopolitical uncertainty, elevated US tariffs and volatile input costs created a challenging operating environment, yet the company continued to expand its manufacturing footprint, strengthen its customer portfolio and invest in new capabilities. The Bengaluru-headquartered apparel manufacturer recorded consolidated total income of around ₹4,065 crore in FY26. The company’s performance reflects a strategy that is increasingly focused not simply on adding production volumes but on building a more diversified, integrated and flexible global manufacturing platform. Investing Ahead of Demand Capacity creation has been one of the most visible elements of Gokaldas Exports’ strategy. The company deployed ₹228 crore of capital expenditure during FY26, of which ₹170 crore went towards new manufacturing facilities and ₹58 crore towards modernisation of existing operations. New capacity in Bhopal and Karnataka is now being progressively ramped up, with both expected to make a meaningful contribution as utilisation increases through FY27. title: BGMEA calls for expanded two-way trade with Pakistan
summary: Mahmud Hasan Khan, President of BGMEA, has urged Pakistan to import more Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceuticals. He said this would help reduce the trade imbalance and strengthen bilateral economic...
content: Mahmud Hasan Khan, President of BGMEA, has urged Pakistan to import more Bangladeshi jute yarn and pharmaceuticals. He said this would help reduce the trade imbalance and strengthen bilateral economic ties. He made the call during a meeting with Pakistan High Commissioner to Bangladesh Imran Haider at the BGMEA office in Dhaka, according to a press release. During the meeting, Mahmud Hasan Khan also called for greater imports of chemicals and dyes from Pakistan for Bangladesh’s garment industry, highlighting opportunities to expand trade in both directions. Bangladesh currently imports a significant volume of products from Pakistan, including raw materials used in the garment sector, while its exports to the Pakistani market remain comparatively low. The BGMEA president stressed the need to address this imbalance by identifying new export opportunities and strengthening commercial links between businesses in the two countries. The Pakistan high commissioner expressed interest in the proposals and assured that necessary steps would be taken to promote bilateral trade. The two sides also discussed arranging visits by high-level business delegations from Bangladesh and Pakistan to identify new business opportunities and establish direct commercial connections. Haider said the Pakistan High Commission would facilitate business-to-business meetings and matchmaking sessions with leading Pakistani importers, brands, buyers and business associations if a Bangladeshi delegation comprising garment and other sector exporters visits Pakistan. The meeting also focused on expanding market access and exploring a possible bilateral preferential trade arrangement to sustain trade flows after Bangladesh graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category. summary: The Japan-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JBCCI) has elected a new 16-member Board of Directors for the 2026–2028 term, with Kazuiki Kataoka taking charge as president. The new board was...
content: The Japan-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (JBCCI) has elected a new 16-member Board of Directors for the 2026–2028 term, with Kazuiki Kataoka taking charge as president. The new board was formally introduced at the chamber’s 21st Annual General Meeting (AGM) held on 4th October at Hotel Lakeshore in Dhaka. Around 240 general members, board members, and distinguished guests from different organisations attended the meeting, which was moderated by JBCCI Executive Director Tahera Ahsan . The election was held on September 23, 2026, with the newly elected office bearers set to serve for the 2026–2028 term. Outgoing President Tareq Rafi Bhuiyan welcomed the participants and spoke about JBCCI’s role in promoting trade and business relations between Bangladesh and Japan. During the AGM, Former Secretary General Maria Howlader FCA presented the chamber’s major activities from November 2025 to September 2026. She said JBCCI’s membership had increased to 391 companies , compared with 369 in the previous year. The rise in membership reflects continued business engagement between companies from Bangladesh and Japan, she said. Former Joint Treasurer Md Jahangir Alam Sharker CPA presented the audited annual financial report. He said the chamber maintained sustainable financial growth while giving attention to transparency, accountability and financial management. The AGM also welcomed new members and approved the appointment of Shafiq Mizan Rahman & Augustine, Chartered Accountants , as the auditor for the 2026–27 financial year. New leadership takes charge Under the new board, Abu Zaman Md. Tariqul Islam and Syed Samiul Huq have been elected vice-presidents, while Rabiul Alam will serve as secretary general. content: On 30 September 2026, a team from Jhpiego Bangladesh paid a courtesy visit to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) to explore opportunities for collaboration in promoting the health, wellbeing, and productivity of RMG workers. The meeting was attended by BGMEA Directors — Fahima Akter and and Rumana Rashid and former BGMEA Director Md. Nazrul Islam, who engaged with the Jhpiego Bangladesh team in a constructive discussion on potential areas of collaboration. The delegation also met with BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan. Jhpiego, a global non-profit health organization and an affiliate of Johns Hopkins University, works to improve the health of women, families, and communities worldwide. Drawing on its experience in the RMG sector, the Jhpiego team shared valuable insights from its programs and study findings, highlighting the important connection between workers’ health, wellbeing, and workplace productivity. Representing Jhpiego Bangladesh were Samiha Yunus, Team Lead – Surveillance, Gazi Md. Rezaul Karim, Program Director – SRHR, Md. Afzal Hossain, Program Specialist and Farzana Khan, Private Sector Engagement Manager. The discussion explored potential avenues for partnership that can help strengthen worker-focused health initiatives and contribute to healthier workers, more productive workplaces, and more resilient factory communities. For more exclusive interviews, stories and opinions from different industry perspectives, and real survey feedback from voices from every level of fashion, download The AI Report 2026 . We’re observing a big disconnect (in both our own fashion-only data and in wider benchmarks from other sources) between the increasing capability and reliability of AI, in both a general sense and in discrete applications, and the lack of trust that end users place in its outputs. What do you think trust in AI looks like, and what’s the right rubric for measuring it? At its best, fashion is human, physical, emotional, and cultural. Being worn on the body, it can create performance, beauty, identity, or all three at once. It can be the Gucci Fashion Show taking over Times Square, with the noise, traffic, billboards, celebrity, commerce, and chaos of New York moving around it. Fashion can be precise and out of control at the same time. That contrast is part of the magic. The outfits are important, but so is the world they enter, the people wearing them, and the meaning a brand creates around them. That is why AI-generated fashion can feel uncomfortable. When people see synthetic models or products that feel assembled by algorithms, they can sense the absence of human intent. content: North Wales manufacturer KnitMesh Technologies is taking its specialist wire knitting technology into the rapidly developing counter-drone market with a stainless steel mesh designed to provide a physical barrier against hostile unmanned aircraft systems (UAS). The company showcased its DroneStop Counter-UAS Shield at the Counter-UAS Homeland Security Europe conference in London on September 30 and October 1, positioning the technology as a passive addition to the electronic detection and jamming systems increasingly being deployed to protect sensitive sites. Established in 1957 and headquartered in Greenfield, Flintshire, KnitMesh Technologies has spent almost 70 years developing knitted wire mesh for applications ranging from automotive components and filtration to hydrogen production, thermal management and industrial safety. It also operates a manufacturing facility near New Delhi, India. Developed, manufactured and tested in the UK, DroneStop employs high-strength stainless steel knitted wire mesh to create a lightweight physical barrier above or around vulnerable assets. Unlike electronic counter-drone systems, it requires no power supply and does not rely on radio-frequency interference or signal jamming. Instead, the mesh is intended to form the final physical layer of a broader counter-UAS strategy, protecting locations including military bases, ammunition and fuel storage areas, aircraft facilities, communications infrastructure, prisons and other critical national infrastructure. The approach reflects the increasing complexity of protecting sites against relatively small and inexpensive unmanned aircraft. title: Germany’s apparel market remains under pressure
summary: Germany’s apparel market experienced notable pressure in 2026, driven by a broader contraction in European clothing imports and surging domestic energy costs. Provisional Eurostat data shows Germany’s...
content: Germany’s apparel market experienced notable pressure in 2026, driven by a broader contraction in European clothing imports and surging domestic energy costs. Provisional Eurostat data shows Germany’s clothing imports from non-EU suppliers fell 17.0% year-over-year in the first half of 2026. Figure: In fiscal year 2025–26, garment exports to Germany totaled $4.38 billion, highlighting the market’s ongoing scale. This downturn coincides with sharp cost increases across the German trade landscape. According to the Federal Statistical Office, import prices jumped 8.3% year-over-year in August 2026, marking the sharpest annual surge since December 2022. Export prices also climbed 4.7% during the same month. A 43.0% spike in imported energy costs served as the primary catalyst for these inflationary pressures. The weakening demand extends beyond Germany to the broader European market. Total EU apparel imports from global suppliers dropped 9.7% year-over-year to €41.1 billion during the first six months of 2026. Import volumes shrank by 6.4%, while average unit prices declined by 3.53%. Despite tightening market conditions, Germany maintains its position as a major European hub for international apparel trade. In fiscal year 2025–26, garment exports to Germany totaled $4.38 billion, highlighting the market’s ongoing scale. Moving forward, dynamic cost structures, shifting consumer demand, and fluctuating energy prices will remain critical factors shaping Germany’s global supply chains and trade stability.

The company shifted its strategic focus to high-quality interlining fabrics in 1974 and subsequently expanded its presence across major garment-producing markets in Asia. content: Bangladesh’s apparel sector is installing rooftop photovoltaic (PV) systems to handle severe gas shortages and grid failures. Reliable electricity is necessary to protect export production. Rooftop solar helps factory owners produce clean energy, lower power costs, and run uninterrupted operations. Assessing industrial rooftop capacity and demand impact The potential for solar generation across the apparel manufacturing landscape is substantial. A detailed assessment by the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) reveals that 3,320 garment factories across the country possess a cumulative rooftop solar potential of 1,768 megawatt-peak (MWp). The study mapped roughly 9.7 million square meters of usable rooftop area. Under optimal setup, solar arrays can meet a median of 39.9% of electricity demand in large factories, 33.1% in medium-sized units, and 38% in small manufacturing facilities. Converting this potential into active capacity requires structured investment. Recent Report data identifies 509 factories as investment-ready, with another 1,359 factories capable of becoming investable with financial support. Installing rooftop systems across 2,303 non-solar factories requires an estimated total investment of $188.2 million. Expanding factory adoption and portfolio targets Factory-level solar deployments are expanding rapidly through experienced engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) providers. Solaric, a major industrial solar installer, reports a portfolio target of 212 MWp in total installations for 2025, which is projected to expand to 400 MWp by 2027. content: Raidha Collections Ltd., one of the largest sister concerns of Labib Group, has appointed its new CEO, Shazia Zaheen Alamgir, daughter of Salahuddin Alamgir and Sultana Jahan, Chairman and Vice Chairman of Labib Group. She has been appointed Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Raidha Collections and has taken charge of the role. Shazia Zaheen Alamgir has been associated with the group’s business activities for a long time as Group Director. During her tenure as Director, she gained experience in Labib Group’s management and business operations. She completed her MYP diploma and IB diploma at International School Dhaka (ISD). She subsequently earned her undergraduate degree from Emerson College in Boston, USA, and her postgraduate degree from City St. george’s, University of London. In her new role, Shazia Zaheen Alamgir will lead overall business operations, with a strong focus on EU business and management of Raidha Collections. At the same time, she will work to further advance the company’s business growth and future initiatives. In her personal life, she is married to Siraajam Munir Khan. Both are associated with City, St George’s, University of London. Siraajam Munir Khan is the son of Ikram Ahmed Khan, Chairman of the Dubai- and Hong Kong-based Shun Shing Group. The facility was inaugurated on 03 October at a ceremony attended by senior executives of Wendler Interlining Group, industry stakeholders and business partners. The opening marks a new phase in the company’s efforts to expand local production and provide faster supply and technical support to Bangladesh’s garment manufacturers. Wendler Interlining is a family-owned German company with a history dating back to 1843. The company evolved from a textile finishing business into a specialist in high-quality interlinings for the garment industry. It established its Bangladesh subsidiary in 2022, building on its production presence in the country since 2009. Speaking at the opening ceremony, Dr Gerhart Wendler, Chairman of Wendler Interlining Group said, “With more than 183 years of heritage, our transformation across successive generations reflects a continuing commitment to innovation and quality. title: Rampal power plant sets new record with 1,321MW generation
summary: The Rampal coal-fired power plant in Bagerhat has generated a record 1,321 megawatts (MW) of electricity, exceeding its combined installed capacity of 1,320MW. At around 4:30pm on October 3, Unit 1 g...
content: The Rampal coal-fired power plant in Bagerhat has generated a record 1,321 megawatts (MW) of electricity, exceeding its combined installed capacity of 1,320MW. At around 4:30pm on October 3, Unit 1 generated 656MW while Unit 2 produced 665MW, bringing the plant’s total generation to 1,321MW. Figure: At around 4:30pm on October 3, Unit 1 generated 656MW while Unit 2 produced 665MW, bringing the plant’s total generation to 1,321MW. According to Anwarul Azim, General Manager of the Rampal Thermal Power Plant, both units are supplying electricity directly to Bangladesh's national grid. “After production was temporarily suspended due to a mechanical fault, the two units are now generating electricity continuously,” he said. He added that electricity from the plant would be supplied to the national grid according to demand. The Rampal power plant, located in Bagerhat, was initiated as a joint venture between Bangladesh and India in 2010. The latest generation milestone comes after both units resumed operations following a mechanical fault, allowing the plant to supply electricity continuously to the national grid.

Organized jointly by WaterAid Bangladesh and BKMEA with support from the Embassy of Sweden in Dhaka, the program brought together […] The post BKMEA inaugurated its Water Cell to strengthen the industry’s role in responsible water management appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: BKMEA inaugurated its Water Cell yesterday (3 October 2026) to strengthen the industry’s role in responsible water management. The inauguration was held alongside an awareness and consultation session on Water Stewardship in Bangladesh’s knitwear sector. Organized jointly by WaterAid Bangladesh and BKMEA with support from the Embassy of Sweden in Dhaka, the program brought together representatives from the knitwear industry, BKMEA and international brands. BKMEA Director Engr. Md. Belayet Hossain represented BKMEA during the inaugural session. The day-long program featured technical discussions and group activities on measuring and reducing water consumption, increasing water reuse and preventing pollution, along with exploring opportunities to develop water-efficiency initiatives into viable and investment-ready projects. In his closing remarks, BKMEA Executive President Ehsan Fazlee Shamim emphasized that water management should not be viewed solely from a business perspective; it is also an ethical responsibility. He highlighted that the impacts of water misuse and pollution ultimately affect our country, communities and people, making responsible water use a collective responsibility. The initiative is expected to strengthen awareness, capacity and collaboration on responsible water management across Bangladesh’s knitwear sector. According to the minister, a tone of raw jute, which reached around Tk150,000, or about $1,200, at peak market prices last year, could generate $2,400–2,500 when processed into packaging products. content: Author: Sultan Mahmud Sohal, Country Manager, Corporate Responsibility, KM International GmbH (Branch office of FLORETT TEXTIL GmbH & Co. KG) Ten years is long enough to change an industry, and it is certainly long enough to leave an imprint on the people who work within it. In Bangladesh, the story of garments and textiles is often presented through export earnings, factory numbers, production capacity, employment and market share. These figures are important because they demonstrate the extraordinary scale of an industry that has become central to the country’s economy and international identity. Yet numbers alone cannot capture what this sector really represents. Behind every shipment is a worker beginning a shift, an engineer solving a production problem, a merchandiser managing a demanding deadline, an entrepreneur taking a financial risk, a technician learning a new machine, or a young professional trying to build a career in an industry that connects Bangladesh with consumers across the world. Behind every factory is a community, and behind every export figure are millions of individual stories. That human dimension is what makes Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry much more than an economic statistic. It is an important part of the country’s social and economic transformation, and for the past ten years, Textile Focus has been one of the dedicated platforms telling that story. title: Sustainable composite buttons from textile waste

summary: A waste-to-value approach using cotton knit waste, wood sawdust and ETP sludge Introduction Buttons are small fastening devices commonly used in clothing and accessories to secure or decorate garments...
content: A waste-to-value approach using cotton knit waste, wood sawdust and ETP sludge Introduction Buttons are small fastening devices commonly used in clothing and accessories to secure or decorate garments. They are usually made from materials like plastic, metal, shell, wood, or resin. Plastic buttons, such as those made from ABS, polyester, and nylon, are popular because they are inexpensive, durable, and easy to design. However, these synthetic materials contribute to microplastic pollution, release harmful chemicals during production, and do not break down naturally. This raises serious environmental concerns [1]. With around 60 billion buttons produced each year, even a slight change to sustainable materials can significantly impact the environment [2] At the same time, the textile and fashion industries significantly harm the environment. They contribute to solid textile waste. Textile Solid Waste (TSW) is categorized into pre-consumer, production, and post-consumer waste. The textile sector generates nearly 5% of all global waste, while millions of tonnes of textile waste are generated and disposed of in landfills each year. [3]. This study explores making composite buttons using waste fabric, wood sawdust, and ETP sludge, with epoxy resin as the binder using the Hand Lay-Up method. Findings show that these waste-based composites could serve as a sustainable and functional alternative to traditional plastic buttons in the textile industry Objectives The goal of this project is to create sustainable composite buttons using leftover textiles and assess how well they work for real-world uses. Sedex’s sample survey found that only 12% of organizations have data from most of their second-tier suppliers. Sedex data shows another gap. About 15% of supply chain worksites have no measures to ensure their suppliers or subcontractors meet required labor standards. The new mapping workflow allows suppliers to add and label upstream connections by tier. The platform also gives buying organizations more detailed risk intelligence. Analytics dashboards can identify higher-risk suppliers by tier and highlight gaps in risk mitigation. Sedex has expanded its risk assessment tools across 15 topics for more than 120,000 registered worksites. The Audit Risk pillar uses findings from more than 250,000 SMETA audits across 115,000 sites in 106 countries. It also incorporates data from the latest SMETA 7.0 standard. Sedex has also upgraded its Wages Risk pillar. It combines wage data from more than 70,000 site-level SMETA audits with external expert sources. A new environmental risk assessment feature brings environmental data together at the worksite level. This can help companies prioritize environmental due diligence across their supplier networks.

title: Patagonia joins ACT to push living wages across apparel supply chains
summary: Patagonia has joined the ACT Initiative, strengthening its focus on living wages through industry-wide collaboration and collective bargaining. Patagonia defines a living wage as income that allows w...
content: Patagonia has joined the ACT Initiative, strengthening its focus on living wages through industry-wide collaboration and collective bargaining. Patagonia defines a living wage as income that allows workers to meet basic needs such as food, housing, healthcare, and education. In many apparel-producing countries, statutory minimum wages remain below these levels. The company has worked on living wages for more than a decade. In 2015, Patagonia set a goal for all workers across its supply chain to earn a living wage by 2025. It also researched wage gaps, worked with suppliers, and introduced programs to support workers. These included supplier education, wage assessments, and Fair Trade mechanisms that provided direct financial benefits to workers. However, Patagonia now says broader economic and policy factors also shape wage outcomes. “For years, our focus was on the actions we could take directly with suppliers and their workers,” said Wendy Savage, Senior Director of Social Impact and Transparency at Patagonia. “What we’ve learned is that lasting wage growth depends on much broader systems, including government policies and industry-wide agreements.” The ACT Initiative, which stands for Action, Collaboration, Transformation, brings together brands, retailers, employer organizations, governments, and the IndustriALL Global Union. Patagonia’s move therefore shifts its living wage strategy from mainly supplier-level programs toward broader industry and country-level action.

content: Saurer Texparts held an ‘In‑Mill Product’ symposium with Saiham Group in Habiganj, Bangladesh. The event brought 45 participants for technical training on its latest spinning components and solutions. The initiative highlighted Saurer Texparts’ focus on direct customer engagement and the practical application of technical knowledge in spinning mills. Led by M Gopi, Global Sales Manager, Saurer Textile Solutions Private Ltd ., the symposium provided participants with technical insights into solutions designed to improve energy efficiency, yarn quality and productivity in spinning operations. Among the technologies discussed was the Spinnfinity and E-Shape spindle, which can reduce energy consumption by up to 6%. The session also covered the PK 2360 SEH, featuring a robust mechanical system with a hexagonal support rod aimed at enhancing yarn quality in spinning machines. Another key solution presented was the RB 105 rotor bearing system, which uses advanced materials to support higher productivity in rotor spinning operations. The training was designed to move beyond theoretical product knowledge by demonstrating how the technologies can be assessed under actual mill conditions. Figure: M Gopi, Global Sales Manager, Saurer Textile Solutions Private Ltd . Following the symposium, Saiham Group is evaluating Texparts solutions in real production environments to assess their performance and suitability for its spinning operations. According to Saurer Texparts, the initiative created an opportunity for technical knowledge exchange while allowing the company to better understand customer requirements and support mills in improving operational performance. Through runway presentations, designer exhibitions, conversations and professional exchange, the event will spotlight the people, ideas and partnerships shaping a more design-led future for Bangladesh. A first platform for a design led Bangladesh Bangladesh is recognised worldwide for its apparel manufacturing capability. Design In Bangladesh Week adds a new dimension to that story by foregrounding original design, contemporary craft, product development, cultural intelligence and brand-building. The platform is designed to help make Bangladesh not only a place where products are made, but a place where new fashion, material and creative ideas are developed and seen. The programme will feature the Designer Discovery Pavilion, a premium fashion exhibition and curated runway showcases. Emerging and established designers will have opportunities to present collections, explore contemporary interpretations of heritage, meet industry professionals and build visibility within the wider textile-apparel value chain. title: Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition targets scale-up of lower-carbon
summary: The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has launched with more than 60 fashion brands, retailers, manufacturers, and innovators to accelerate the commercial adoption of lower-carbon materials and product...
content: The Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition has launched with more than 60 fashion brands, retailers, manufacturers, and innovators to accelerate the commercial adoption of lower-carbon materials and production technologies. Figure: Climate Pledge Fashion Coalition will focus on organic, recycled, and next-generation fibers. The coalition was launched on September 23, 2026, by The Climate Pledge, Amazon, Stella McCartney and Canopy, with convening support from the World Economic Forum. It aims to address one of fashion’s biggest sustainability barriers. This moves proven solutions from small-scale innovation to commercial production. The initiative will focus on organic, recycled and next-generation fibers. It will also support manufacturing technologies that can reduce water use, chemical inputs and greenhouse gas emissions. According to Global Fashion Agenda and McKinsey, the fashion industry generated about 2.1 billion tons of greenhouse gas emissions in 2018. Around 70% came from upstream activities such as materials production, preparation and processing. The coalition is therefore targeting the supply chain earlier in the product lifecycle instead of focusing mainly on garment reuse, recycling and disposal. The initiative builds on the wider Climate Pledge network, which now includes more than 700 signatories across more than 60 industries. Its members are committed to reaching net-zero carbon by 2040. Fashion-focused participants include Anna Sui, Another Tomorrow, Bananatex, Brooks Running, Circ, DL1961, E.L.V Denim, Mother Denim, Selfridges, unspun and Vestiaire Collective. For fashion manufacturers, this could gradually expand access to lower-impact fibers and technologies beyond limited pilot projects.

title: Stakeholders’ Dialogue on Ending Digital & AI-Facilitated Violence Against Women
summary: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Stakeholders’ Dialogue and Preparatory Workshop on Ending Digital Violence Against Women, held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon, brought together policymakers, parliamentarians and civil society leaders to address the rapidly growing threat of AI-enabled harassment, abuse and exploitation of women and children. The session was moderated by Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asad […] The post Stakeholders’ Dialogue on Ending Digital & AI-Facilitated Violence Against Women appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ Stakeholders’ Dialogue and Preparatory Workshop on Ending Digital Violence Against Women, held at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon, brought together policymakers, parliamentarians and civil society leaders to address the rapidly growing threat of AI-enabled harassment, abuse and exploitation of women and children. The session was moderated by Foreign Secretary Ambassador Asad Alam Siam, with remarks from Hon’ble State Minister for Foreign Affairs Ms. Shama Obaed Islam, MP; Hon’ble State Minister for Social Welfare Ms. Farzana Sharmin Putul, MP; Hon’ble Minister for Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs Md. Asaduzzaman, MP; Barrister Jahrat Adib Chowdhury, MP; and Ms. Sanjida Islam Tulee, MP. Speaking at the dialogue, Vidiya Amrit Khan, Vice President, BGMEA, stressed that addressing digital and AI-facilitated violence must begin with a broader change in society, culture and mindset towards women. She highlighted the silence surrounding domestic and child sexual abuse, the social taboos that prevent survivors from seeking help, and the urgent need for stronger implementation of existing laws. She called for educating children from an early age to respect women and recognise their value, alongside stronger enforcement, AI safeguards and age-appropriate regulation of children’s access to social media. She further emphasised that, as a Muslim woman, she believes Islam unequivocally upholds the dignity, rights and respect of women. The meeting was part of Bangladesh government’s work to establish the Dhaka Dialogue, a government-led platform introduced at the 10th Dakar International Forum on Peace and Security in Africa on 20 April 2026. content: At a CCEA meeting on Thursday, the government gave final approval to a draft 15-year concession agreement with an international terminal operator. The government has decided to hand over the operation and maintenance of Chattogram Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and its overflow yard (OCY) to a foreign operator. At a meeting of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) chaired by Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury on Thursday, final approval was given to a draft 15-year concession agreement with an international terminal operator. According to a proposal submitted by the Ministry of Shipping, Chattogram Port Authority (CPA) will sign the agreement under a project titled “Operation and Maintenance of Chattogram Port Authority’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) and Overflow Yard (OCY)” under a public-private partnership (PPP) project. Meanwhile, the CCEA gave in-principle approval to another proposal submitted by the industries ministry. Under the proposal, urea fertiliser will be imported from Russian fertiliser manufacturer JSC Shchekinoazot through a direct procurement method (DPM) via UAE-based Delta Star Trading FZ-LLC. content: From pioneering India’s Overhead Travelling Cleaner more than five decades ago to developing intelligent automation systems for modern spinning mills, ELGI Electric is now making automation the next major chapter in its engineering journey. V.S. Balasubramanian, President-Operations , ELGI Electric “Whenever we introduced a new product, we never compromised on technology. We first identified the best technology available anywhere in the world and then worked towards making it even better for Indian customers. That philosophy has remained unchanged throughout our journey.” This philosophy perhaps best explains both the longevity of ELGI Electric Industries Ltd. and the direction in which the Coimbatore-based engineering company is now heading. For more than six decades, ELGI Electric has built its reputation by identifying emerging technologies, adapting them to Indian textile manufacturing and continuously refining them in close collaboration with customers. Its pioneering introduction of the Overhead Travelling Cleaner (OHTC) to India established the company’s position in textile machinery. Subsequent developments in yarn conditioning, fire and metal detection and Bobbin Transportation Systems expanded that engineering base. Today, however, the opportunity is considerably larger. As textile manufacturing becomes increasingly automated, connected and data-driven, ELGI Electric is moving beyond individual machines towards integrated automation solutions that connect processes, reduce manual intervention and improve productivity. The shift is being driven by a fundamental change in the industry’s requirements. title: 틸아이다이, 포근한 텍스처로 풀어낸 26 WINTER 컬렉션

summary: 언노운네이처의 착색 케어 브랜드 아윌미백은 우주글로벌과 중국 총판 계약을 체결했다.아윌미백 측에 따르면 ‘뱀파이어 톤업 스프레이’는 지난 7월 중국 왕홍 따따의 라이브 방송에서 준비 물량이 약 2시간 만에 소진됐다. 브랜드는 해당 기간 더우인 주간 판매 1위를 기록했으며 이후 수만 개 단위 추가 물량을 현지에 공급했다고 밝혔다.우주글로벌은 지난 6월부터 해당 제품의 중국 물량 공급을 담당해 왔으며 이번 계약을 통해 공식 총판 역할을 맡는다. 양사는 온라인 판매를 중심으로 유통을 운영한 뒤 오프라인 채널까지 단계적으로 확대할 계획이다

summary: 더퓨처는 2026년 1~3분기 글로벌본부 매출이 전년 동기 대비 841% 증가했다고 밝혔다.회사 집계 기준 약 9.4배 수준으로, 국가별 제품 운영과 이커머스 채널 확대가 매출 증가에 영향을 미쳤다는 설명이다. 중국에서는 현지 소비자 수요를 반영한 제품과 마케팅을 운영하고 있으며 일본에서는 이너뷰티 브랜드 ‘낫띵베럴’을 중심으로 큐텐 등 이커머스 채널에서 판매하고 있다.미국에서는 틱톡샵을 활용한 판매와 콘텐츠 운영을 진행하고 있다. 항노화 뷰티 브랜드 EOA의 글로벌 플랫폼 입점도 단계적으로 추진한다. 내년 1월 ‘CES 2027’

summary: 향수 브랜드 히어로즈 오브 코리아는 10월 2일부터 15일까지 갤러리아백화점 명품관 WEST 5층에서 팝업스토어를 운영한다.이번 팝업은 향수 시향과 민화 전시를 결합했다. 히어로즈 오브 코리아의 향에서 연상되는 꽃과 문방사우 등 한국적 소재를 민화로 재해석했으며, 작품 제작에는 갤러리 일백헌이 참여했다. 특정 역사적 인물을 직접 묘사하기보다 조향사가 향으로 구성한 이야기를 작가가 시각적 이미지로 옮기는 방식이다.방문객은 향을 시향한 뒤 작품을 감상하고 다시 향을 경험할 수 있도록 공간을 구성했다. 브랜드는 이를 통해 후각 중심의 향

title: Six forces reweaving the future of global textiles
title_ko: 글로벌 섬유의 미래를 엮는 6가지 힘
summary: For decades, the global textile industry followed a simple formula: make more, make it faster and make it cheaper. That formula built enormous manufacturing hubs, expanded global sourcing networks and...
content: For decades, the global textile industry followed a simple formula: make more, make it faster and make it cheaper. That formula built enormous manufacturing hubs, expanded global sourcing networks and made polyester the workhorse of modern textiles. But the formula is changing. Global fiber production reached a record 132 million tons in 2024 , up from around 125 million tons in 2023. Production has more than doubled since 2000 and under business-as-usual conditions could reach approximately 169 million tons by 2030 . Courtesy: Collected The industry is being pushed to use different materials, reduce waste, automate production, prove its claims and build supply chains that can withstand disruption. Six forces are changing this transition: man-made fibers, circularity, AI and automation, traceability, supply-chain regionalization and advanced materials. Together, they are rewriting the economics of textiles. MMFs If one fiber defines the modern textile economy, it is polyester. Polyester represented around 59% of global fiber production in 2024 , with output rising from approximately 71 million tons in 2023 to about 78 million tons in 2024. Yet around 88% of polyester remained fossil-based . That creates one of the industry's biggest contradictions. Sustainability ambitions are growing while dependence on virgin synthetic materials continues to increase. Replacing polyester entirely is unlikely to happen quickly. Its durability, affordability, versatility and performance have made it indispensable across sportswear, outerwear, home textiles and everyday apparel. Then what will the next generation of polyester be made from? title: AI Labs Keep Demoing The Weirdest Fashion Use Cases
summary: The latest marketing push into always-on AI agents featured fashion, again. But the big labs keep showcasing brand-owners and professionals who seem to want to care less and delegate everything. The more useful promise is the ability to care more: freeing time and attention to improve the product. The post AI Labs Keep Demoing The Weirdest Fashion Use Cases appeared first on The Interline .
content: [Featured image using Dots artwork for inspiration.] Key Takeaways: For the second time in as many months, OpenAI has released a new product with a fashion workflow featured prominently in the accompanying demo. These hypothetical workflows keep presenting an odd window into the reality of AI deployments and the likely real sources of ROI for actual fashion businesses, and the incentives are difficult to decipher. Market data presented by a16z and The Interline’s own survey examine different aspects of AI uptake and measurement, with some correlation showing that AI adoption needs to translate into demonstrable product outcomes – especially if agentic commerce ends up de-emphasising website visits. In a new attempt at “sherlocking,” OpenAI launched its own virtual try-on service that hooks into its own in-app shopping experiences and into the company’s new play to become users’ default operating environment. title: Bangladesh exports rise 8.54% in September as RMG shipments recover
summary: Key insights September merchandise exports rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion. RMG exports increased 8.56% to $3.08 billion, with both knitwear and woven garments posting annual growth. Septemb...
content: Key insights September merchandise exports rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion. RMG exports increased 8.56% to $3.08 billion, with both knitwear and woven garments posting annual growth. September exports fell 11.11% from August, showing weaker month-on-month momentum. RMG accounted for about 78.30% of total export earnings in September. Jute, leather and home textiles added strength to the wider export basket. Figure: Export earnings rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion from $3.63 billion in September 2025. Bangladesh’s merchandise exports maintained year-on-year growth in September, although export earnings declined sharply from the previous month. Export earnings rose 8.54% year-on-year to $3.94 billion from $3.63 billion in September 2025, according to the latest Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) data. RMG remains the main export engine Table 1. Bangladesh’s RMG export performance in September 2026 Category September 2025 ($ Billion) September 2026 ($ Billion) Growth Rate (YoY) Knitwear 1.86 2.02 +8.58% Woven garments 0.98 1.06 +8.54% Total RMG 2.84 3.08 +8.56% Total exports 3.63 3.94 +8.54% Source: Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) The RMG sector accounted for about 78.30% of Bangladesh’s total merchandise export earnings in September. RMG exports reached $3.08 billion, up 8.56% from $2.84 billion a year earlier. Within the sector, knitwear and woven garments both recorded year-on-year growth of 8.58% and 8.54%, respectively. The quarterly data also show that knitwear remained the larger apparel segment. During July-September, knitwear exports reached $5.96 billion, up 6.88%, while woven garment exports stood at $4.61 billion, representing 5.11% growth. title: Rieter announces Daniel Lippuner as new CEO
summary: Swiss textile machinery manufacturer Rieter has announced Daniel Lippuner as its new CEO. The leadership transition happened as Thomas Oetterli is stepping down from the CEO role, effective October 31...
content: Swiss textile machinery manufacturer Rieter has announced Daniel Lippuner as its new CEO. The leadership transition happened as Thomas Oetterli is stepping down from the CEO role, effective October 31, 2026, and handing over the chairmanship of the company’s Board of Directors. Figure: Daniel Lippuner new CEO of Rieter Daniel Lippuner will become CEO of Rieter on November 1, 2026. He brings extensive international leadership experience and industry knowledge, particularly in textile machinery and components. Oetterli said the decision follows the successful implementation of Rieter’s Next Level performance program, structural measures to consolidate the company’s sites and the acquisition of Barmag. “After the successful implementation of the Next Level performance program, the structural measures initiated to consolidate the sites and the acquisition of Barmag, the time has come to hand over responsibility to new hands,” Oetterli said. The separation of the CEO and Board Chairman roles had been planned since Oetterli took office. Daniel previously served as CEO of the Saurer Group and headed Oerlikon Textile Components, where he was involved in businesses covering spinning machinery, yarn processing and textile components. He also served as Chairman of the Board and co-owner of Heberlein Technology, maintaining close ties with the chemical fiber industry. His experience in transformation, technology and quality management, operational leadership and Asian markets is expected to support Rieter as the company expands beyond its traditional short-staple fiber business. Carl Illi will serve as Chairman of Rieter’s Board of Directors until the company’s next Annual General Meeting on April 14, 2027. title: Is the biomass boiler boom creating Bangladesh’s next environmental problem?
summary: No gas, expensive diesel—Will our forests, soil, and air burn in the race for alternative fuels? Bangladesh’s industries, especially garments and textiles, face gas shortages, unreliable supplies,...
content: No gas, expensive diesel—Will our forests, soil, and air burn in the race for alternative fuels? Bangladesh’s industries, especially garments and textiles, face gas shortages, unreliable supplies, and rising energy costs. Diesel has risen from Tk 97.5 to Tk 135 per liter, natural gas costs Tk 26.09 per cubic meter excluding VAT, and LPG Tk 108 per kilogram. Many factories have already reduced production because of gas and electricity shortages. Entrepreneurs are therefore turning to LPG, diesel, and biomass boilers. But if we escape a fuel crisis by creating an environmental crisis, society will pay the price. Biomass: Solution or new crisis? Biomass boilers are spreading rapidly, especially chain-grate and fixed-grate models. Biomass could reduce fossil-fuel dependence if it uses sustainable agricultural and natural waste. The key question is: Do we have enough sustainable biomass? Installing a boiler is easy. Securing fuel for the next 10 years is much harder. Is rice husk enough? In Bangladesh, a huge amount of rice husk is used in rice bran oil manufacturing facilities and rice mills, where it is used for heating and steam generation. Biomass boilers had long been used in rice mills before being introduced to the textile industry in Bangladesh. Rice husk has a typical calorific value of about 3,000 kcal/kg, depending on its moisture content and composition. Due to its low calorific value, a huge quantity is required, which is not cost-effective. To increase the calorific value, they may mix rice husk with wood chips, sawdust, and wood. This raises a serious question: Where will the extra wood come from? Bangladesh’s forests are already under pressure. summary: EURATEX has joined a broad coalition of European industry organisations calling on the upcoming Circular Economy Act to establish a stronger and more harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). In a joint position paper, the signatories underline that the Circular Economy Act should help Europe move from fragmented national waste management systems towards… Read more The post EURATEX calls for a harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility appeared first on EURATEX .
content: EURATEX has joined a broad coalition of European industry organisations calling on the upcoming Circular Economy Act to establish a stronger and more harmonised EU framework for Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). In a joint position paper, the signatories underline that the Circular Economy Act should help Europe move from fragmented national waste management systems towards a functioning Single Market for secondary raw materials . Extended Producer Responsibility already plays a central role in financing the collection, sorting and recycling of waste across Europe. However, different national approaches and administrative requirements continue to create complexity for companies operating across borders and can limit the development of circular value chains. A more harmonised European approach The coalition therefore calls for a horizontal EU EPR Regulation , establishing a common baseline for EU-mandated EPR schemes while allowing sector-specific requirements where needed. Such an approach would help reduce regulatory fragmentation, provide greater legal certainty and support the scaling-up of circular business models and cross-border markets for secondary raw materials. The paper also stresses that EPR systems should remain producer-led . Producers should retain responsibility for decision-making alongside their obligation to finance end-of-life management, while public authorities provide appropriate oversight. Producer contributions should remain dedicated to the collection, sorting and recycling systems for which they were raised. Transparency, simpler rules and investment in recycling Greater transparency across the entire waste management chain is another key priority. summary: Kraig Biocraft Laboratories has shipped its first commercial order of recombinant spider silk yarn, marking a significant step towards the use of the company’s technology in performance textiles. The custom-engineered yarn was produced to fulfil a purchase commitment from an unnamed global performance sports brand and will now be developed into a new performance textile. […] The post Kraig Labs ships first commercial spider silk yarn appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Kraig Biocraft Laboratories has shipped its first commercial order of recombinant spider silk yarn, marking a significant step towards the use of the company’s technology in performance textiles. The custom-engineered yarn was produced to fulfil a purchase commitment from an unnamed global performance sports brand and will now be developed into a new performance textile. The shipment forms part of a confidential pilot development programme targeting the athletic apparel market. Kraig Labs said the yarn has been custom processed to the customer’s specifications, with the initial volume intentionally kept small for the precision application. “Completing the delivery of this spider silk yarn is a huge milestone for Kraig Labs,” said Kim Thompson, founder and CEO of Kraig Labs. “The volume is small by design. This is a precision application, not a bulk order.” Kraig Labs’ technology uses genetically engineered silkworms incorporating key spider silk proteins to produce recombinant spider silk. The company believes the resulting combination of strength, flexibility, toughness and low weight makes the material particularly suited to demanding performance applications. The commercial shipment follows the company’s work to move its spider silk technology from development and scaled production towards customer-led textile applications. Kraig Labs sees elite performance apparel as a potentially important proving ground for the technology, where improvements in strength-to-weight ratio, durability and other material properties can translate directly into product performance. “High-performance sport is where materials prove themselves,” Thompson said. “Performance wins. Organized by the BUTEX Science Club, the day-long event will begin at 8:00 am and continue until evening. […] The post Texverse 2.0 to be held at BUTEX on October 30 appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: The Bangladesh University of Textiles (BUTEX) will host the national competition ‘Texverse 2.0’ on October 30, bringing together students from universities, textile engineering colleges, and higher secondary institutions for competitions focused on research, innovation, creativity, and problem-solving. Organized by the BUTEX Science Club, the day-long event will begin at 8:00 am and continue until evening. Different segments of the competition will be held at the university’s Auditorium, Seminar Room, Academic Building, and Central Field, while some competitions will be conducted online. The event has so far established collaboration with 25 student clubs and organizations from different universities and textile colleges across the country. title: Tencel market heads toward $6.15 billion as lyocell demand accelerates
title_ko: lyocell 수요가 가속화됨에 따라 Tencel 시장은 61억 5천만 달러로 향합니다.
summary: The global Tencel fiber products market is expanding as apparel brands and textile manufacturers increase their use of lower-impact cellulosic fibers. According to Verified Market Reports, the market...
content: The global Tencel fiber products market is expanding as apparel brands and textile manufacturers increase their use of lower-impact cellulosic fibers. According to Verified Market Reports, the market was valued at $3.5 billion in 2025. It is projected to reach $6.15 billion by 2033, growing at a 7.8% CAGR from 2026 to 2033. The growth is supported by demand for sustainable materials, stronger traceability requirements and advances in fiber technology. Tencel products include Lyocell and Modal fibers, which are used across apparel, home textiles and technical applications. A separate 2026 market analysis gives a more detailed view of the fabric segment. According to PW Consulting, the Tencel fiber fabric market reached $3.67 billion in 2025 and could reach $5.94 billion by 2032, at a 7.15% CAGR. Lyocell fiber fabric held the largest share at 59.8%. Apparel remains the largest end-use segment. Apparel and clothing generated about $2.37 billion, or 64.7% of the Tencel fiber fabric market, in 2025. Home textiles followed with $927.7 million, or 25.3%. Technical textiles accounted for $365.4 million, or 10%. Asia-Pacific remains the largest regional market. It generated about $1.64 billion in Tencel fiber fabric revenue in 2025. Europe followed at $929.8 million, while North America reached $656.8 million. The broader fiber market also shows stronger demand for regenerated cellulose. According to Lenzing, global production of lyocell, modal, and viscose increased about 4% to 8.7 million tons in 2025. content: The 52nd International Conference of the International Federation of Knitting Technologists (IFKT) is taking place in Zagreb, Croatia, from 30 September to 2 October 2026, bringing together specialists from industry, academia and research. Organised by the Croatian section of IFKT in collaboration with the University of Zagreb, the international meeting combines technical presentations and poster sessions with opportunities for discussion and networking among knitting professionals. The conference programme began on Wednesday 30 September at the University of Zagreb Faculty of Textile Technology with a meeting of the IFKT Central Board followed by the organisation’s General Assembly. The technical conference programme opened on Thursday 1 October at Zagreb’s Nikola Tesla Technical Museum. Following registration and the opening ceremony, Zlatko Vrljičak delivered the introductory lecture, Employment in the Croatian Textile and Clothing Industry: With Special Emphasis on the Knitwear Industry . The first oral session focuses on technology, materials and characterisation and is chaired by Marcus O. Weber. Among the opening presentations is Cotton Grass Fibers – Textile Technological Approach , delivered by Marc Küperkoch. Thomas Mutschler and Marc Küperkoch are also presenting research into component optimisation for high-speed yarn guiding elements designed for processing highly abrasive yarns at high speeds. The work examines ceramic materials and high-frequency vibrations. The programme continues through 2 October, with the conference providing a platform for sharing developments in knitting technology, materials, textile engineering and associated research. content: DHAKA – Bangladesh is set to quadruple polyester-chip capacity at a local producer, in a bid to reduce reliance on imported synthetic textile inputs. The move comes as garment makers seek to expand beyond cotton and move into new product segments. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has signed a US$50mloan with Modern Syntex Limited, part of TK Group, to expand its polyester-chip manufacturing operation in the Mirsarai Economic Zone near Chattogram. The project will increase the plant’s capacity from 107 tonnes to 407 tonnes a day. It is designed to produce high-intrinsic-viscosity polyester chips for higher-value textile and apparel applications, with commercial operations targeted for 2027. The investment comes as Bangladesh’s garment industry remains heavily weighted towards cotton, while manufacturers look to capture more orders for man-made-fibre products. Industry estimates put man-made-fibre apparel at about 25 per cent of Bangladesh’s garment export revenues, compared with around 70 per cent of global clothing consumption. Polyester demand in Bangladesh is estimated to be growing by about 10 per cent a year. The Business Standard reported in September that annual local demand is around 140,000–160,000 tonnes for polyester staple fibre, while demand for polyester yarn is estimated at 500,000–550,000 tonnes. The same report said Modern Syntex already produces polyester staple fibre, filament yarn and PET chips, and meets nearly 21% of the country’s demand for polyester products. It also reported that a significant share of domestic demand is still met through imports. The ADB-backed expansion is therefore part of a broader effort to build domestic capacity, rather than Bangladesh’s first move into polyester production. title_ko: Senbis 바이오플라스틱 연구원을 위한 Paul Schlack 상
summary: Momo Naeimirad of Netherlands-based Senbis Polymer Innovations has received the 2026 Paul Schlack Prize for research into the relationship between the performance and biodegradation of melt-spun bioplastic fibres. Presented at the 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress held in Austria from September 16-18, the award recognised Naeimirad’s PolyBioDeg research into how the structure and properties of […] The post Paul Schlack Prize for Senbis bioplastics researcher appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: Momo Naeimirad of Netherlands-based Senbis Polymer Innovations has received the 2026 Paul Schlack Prize for research into the relationship between the performance and biodegradation of melt-spun bioplastic fibres. Presented at the 65th Dornbirn Global Fiber Congress held in Austria from September 16-18, the award recognised Naeimirad’s PolyBioDeg research into how the structure and properties of melt-spun bioplastic fibres influence both their mechanical performance during use and their subsequent biodegradation. Naeimirad is affiliated with Senbis and the University of Amsterdam. The Paul Schlack Prize is one of the fibre industry’s longest-established awards for young researchers. First awarded in 1971 and named after Paul Schlack, the inventor of polyamide 6, it is intended to encourage research and development in the manufacture, processing and application of man-made fibres in Europe. The €3,000 prize is awarded annually at Dornbirn following assessment by an independent jury. Naeimirad’s work addresses an increasingly important challenge for biodegradable polymers – achieving the mechanical and processing performance required during a product’s useful life while ensuring that the material can subsequently biodegrade under appropriate environmental conditions. It is an issue closely related to the wider development programme of Senbis at its base in Emmen, the Netherlands. The company used Dornbirn’s Innovation Day and Forum to present its GreenPearls range of biodegradable compounds for fibre and filament production. The materials are being engineered specifically around individual fibre-forming processes, with the aim of overcoming some of the processing and performance limitations traditionally associated with biodegradable polymers. content: With its state-of-the-art manufacturing facility in Ranipet now fully operational, AMANN Group is moving into a new phase of growth in India—combining global thread expertise with local manufacturing, faster delivery, application support and a growing portfolio of sustainable and high-performance solutions. Sanjeev Grewal, Regional Business Director – Asia, Middle East & Pacific , Amann Group For AMANN Group, India is no longer simply another market in its global network. It is emerging as a strategically important manufacturing and consumption centre, with opportunities extending across apparel, home textiles, footwear, leather and technical applications. The German thread specialist, which began its Indian journey with a trading operation in Chennai in 2007, has now taken a significant step forward by establishing a modern manufacturing facility at Ranipet in Tamil Nadu. The transformation reflects AMANN’s confidence in the long-term potential of the Indian textile and allied industries. After spending years understanding the market, its customers and their requirements, the company commenced construction of the Ranipet plant in 2022. Commercial production began towards the end of 2024, following a two-year delay caused by the pandemic. The facility has since completed its ramp-up phase and is now fully equipped to serve the Indian market with AMANN’s portfolio of products. For Sanjeev Grewal, Regional Business Director – Asia, Middle East & Pacific, the manufacturing investment represents much more than localisation. It is a clear expression of AMANN’s long-term commitment to India. From Trading to Manufacturing AMANN’s Indian journey began with a trading company in Chennai. The demonstration puts a robotic hand to work with one of the most delicate and deformable materials it can encounter. […] The post Getting to grips with silk appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: A robotic hand developed by Chinese firm Agilink has been taught foundational Suzhou embroidery techniques by master craftswoman Fu Xianghong, including separating silk threads, threading a needle, stretching fabric on an embroidery hoop and stitching. The demonstration puts a robotic hand to work with one of the most delicate and deformable materials it can encounter. A silk thread can bend, slip and change shape with slight changes in contact. Splitting silk requires one finger to separate individual strands while others maintain support and tension. Twisting thread meanwhile requires opposing fingertips to maintain contact while allowing the thread to turn. Threading a needle and stitching add further demands on positioning, force and coordination. The OmniHand 3 Ultra combines 21 active degrees of freedom with a fully direct-drive architecture and tactile sensing across the fingertips, finger pads and palm. Vision-based tactile sensors at each fingertip detect changes in the contact surface, providing feedback as the hand handles thin, deformable materials. “A single silk thread gives OmniHand 3 Ultra’s fingertip dexterity a visible measure,” said Qiao Tianjie, vice president of Agibot and CEO of Agilink. “It also reveals the possibility of handing more delicate work to machines.” The demonstration comes as Agilink reaches a new stage of commercial scale. Spun out from Agibot in January 2026, the company has shipped more than 15,000 dexterous hands to date. In August, its OmniHand series competed across all eight dexterous-hand events at the World Humanoid Robot Games, winning seven gold, four silver and three bronze medals. content: Urmi Group has launched an initiative to make its drivers more careful on the road, placing drawings and short messages from drivers' children on the back of its goods-carrying vehicles. Garment factories and other industrial units use thousands of trucks, covered vans and pickups every day to move goods. According to 2023 data from the Bangladesh Road Transport Authority (BRTA), 1,389 trucks and covered vans and 370 pickups were among the 7,837 vehicles involved in road accidents, nearly 22 percent of the total. On Urmi Group's vehicles, each drawing carries one message: the father should drive carefully and return home safe at the end of the day. Some pictures show family stories, others a child's love for their father. The initiative draws on the "Children's Museum Project" of Japanese transport company Miyata Unyu. After a fatal road accident, the company began displaying drivers' children's drawings on its trucks. It reported that accidents fell by around 40 percent after drawings were added to 87 vehicles over six years. In 2019, the project became an independent organization and spread to many companies across Japan. In Bangladesh, painting pictures, slogans and artwork on the back of trucks is a long-standing tradition. Urmi Group is using this familiar space to build an emotional bond between drivers and their families. The group also believes the drawings will carry a humane message to pedestrians and other drivers. Urmi Group Managing Director Asif Ashraf said he experienced the idea first-hand while attending a seminar in Japan, and it moved him personally. "A child's drawing constantly reminds a driver that a family is waiting for him to return home safely," he said.
